explanation.overall:
The hook is built around a hole. He lands the title phrase at 0:41 — a complete, finished confession, no object, no excuse — and then the song makes you wait 6.8 seconds before the condition arrives at 0:48. That gap isn't a pause; it's the whole idea. For seven seconds the line means "I am unwell." Then the second half lands and retroactively rewrites it into "only when you're gone." The song runs this exact move four times (0:41→0:48, 0:59→1:06, 1:53→2:00, 2:11→2:18), always the same length. You learn to dread the silence, because you know what it's about to blame.

The machine underneath is density, not volume. Verse two crams syllables in — the lines at 1:19 and 1:30 are mouthfuls, rationalizing at speed — while the chorus has almost no words in it at all. And the measured clip shows the floor is busy the whole time: an attack every ~0.35 seconds (2.83 per second) under a voice holding notes across seven-second gaps. Busy floor, still ceiling. That's why the empty stretches read as exhaustion rather than as space — the track is still frantic while he's stopped talking.

Two more measured tells. The clip's loudest instant comes early (0.91 at 4.3s) and nothing afterward beats it — the section works by carving away and slamming back, not by piling on, and the two deep interior dips (0.33, then 0.29) sit about 6.4 seconds apart, roughly a two-bar clock at the felt tempo. Meanwhile brightness climbs steadily across the thirty seconds (1677 → 1849 → 1897 Hz) without the loudness rising: the record gets sharper, not bigger. That's the sound of a voice moving into rasp — more edge, same size. (On tempo: librosa reads 156 BPM, which is the fast inner subdivision; the body of the song leans at half that, around 78 — a slow soul stride with a nervous flicker inside it.)

moments.what_happens: Energy jumps from 0.48 to 0.65 at 3.9s and the curve tops out at 0.91 at 4.3s — the highest value anywhere in the thirty seconds. Nothing later reaches it (the next best is 0.89).
moments.why_it_hits: The section shows you its maximum almost immediately, so everything after has to work by taking things away instead of adding them. You stop waiting for a bigger moment and start feeling the loss of the one you already had.

moments.what_happens: Energy bottoms at 0.29 — the lowest interior point in the clip — then the biggest measured rise of the thirty seconds fires at 21.7s (0.59 → 0.79) and keeps climbing to 0.78 by 25.7s. The same collapse-and-return happened 6.4 seconds earlier at 15.0s (0.33 → rise at 15.2s), which is about two bars at the song's felt pulse.
moments.why_it_hits: The floor drops out from under the voice and catches it again on a fixed cycle, so the falling never resolves into landing — you get the stomach-drop twice in six seconds. It's the physical version of the lyric: dropping, being caught, dropping again.

moments.what_happens: "I lose control" arrives at 0:41.62. The line that completes it doesn't come until 0:48.44 — 6.8 seconds of no words. The song repeats this identical delay every time the hook comes around.
moments.why_it_hits: For seven seconds it's a flat confession with no one to blame. Then the condition lands and the meaning flips into an accusation. You feel him hold the shame alone before he hands it over.

moments.what_happens: The verse chains its own vocabulary: "Problematic" seeds "problem is" in the next breath, then "bad habit" seeds "bad habits" in the line after. Lines land 2–4 seconds apart with far more syllables each than anything in the chorus.
moments.why_it_hits: Each word pulls the next one out of it, so the writing itself can't stop — which is exactly what he's describing. And the sudden fast talking after all that chorus silence sounds like someone explaining themselves too quickly to be believed.

moments.what_happens: In the first two choruses, "next to me" is the lead line and "here with me" is the answering backing vocal behind it. In the final chorus, the backing version becomes the lead — the answer has replaced the call.
moments.why_it_hits: The voice that was supporting him is now the only one left, so the last chorus sounds like a man who has absorbed his own backup singers. Something that used to answer him doesn't need to anymore.

explanation.lyric_read: The writing keeps moving the same image from one body to another. In verse one he's the one doing the damage, trying not to tear the skin off his own bones; by verse two the skin has changed owner — "my skin in your teeth." Same picture, self-harm handed over to someone else, which is the whole argument of the song compressed into one recurring noun. The addiction frame (fiend, habit, addict, relief) never once gets called a metaphor, and the one line that admits he could manage alone is immediately overruled by wanting something that requires two people — the rationalization is written into the sentence structure, not stated. And the song's last gesture is a stretch: in the first chorus, "breakin' my heart" and the line after it are 3 seconds apart; in the final chorus, that same last line is held off for nearly 10 seconds (3:17 → 3:27) and then left as the last thing you hear, with nothing after it to answer.
explanation.headline: He sings the title, then withholds the reason for seven seconds — four times.

suggestions.title: Take Me to Church
suggestions.why: Runs the same density engine: verses packed with fast conversational syllables, then a chorus that dumps the words entirely for long held vowels — the contrast, not the volume, is what lifts it.

suggestions.title: Human
suggestions.why: Same drop-and-catch arrangement move — the band clears out from under a rasp-forward belt and slams back on a short fixed cycle, so the hook lands as recovery rather than as a build.

suggestions.title: Tennessee Whiskey
suggestions.why: Builds its entire lyric on the person-as-substance metaphor that verse two runs on (addict, habit, relief), and rides the same half-time lean: sustained vocal over a steady busy subdivision.
